materialIndexBench.title: There is no strongest material
materialIndexBench.subtitle: Twelve materials, four jobs — choosing the job reshuffles the ranking
materialIndexBench.aria: Materials ranked by their performance for the job: {job}
materialIndexBench.jobLabel: What the part has to do
materialIndexBench.legend: Teal bars are grown by an organism; grey bars are manufactured.

hint.tie: A bowstring or a tendon: pure tension, so what matters is strength per unit weight.
hint.beam: A wing spar or a branch: it has to stay stiff in bending, which favours the square root of stiffness over density.
hint.column: A trunk carrying its own weight: buckling sets the limit, and the cube root of stiffness over density decides it.
hint.spring: A bow limb or an ankle tendon: the job is to take energy in and give it back, which rewards strength squared over stiffness.

verdict.tie: Silk sits beside aerospace carbon fibre and leaves steel at the bottom of the board. Weight for weight, a spider outperforms a steel mill.
verdict.beam: Balsa wins, and it is not a trick: for holding a shape against bending per unit weight, a light stiff foam beats every metal here. This is why wings are built hollow.
verdict.column: The same light woods lead again. A trunk fails by buckling, and buckling rewards bulk that weighs nothing — which is exactly what a cellular solid is.
verdict.spring: Now silk is alone at the top, an order of magnitude clear. A bow limb is an energy store, and this is why the good ones are grown rather than cast.

toughnessArchitectureLab.title: The same mineral, arranged four ways
toughnessArchitectureLab.subtitle: Nothing about the ingredient changes — only where it is put
toughnessArchitectureLab.aria: A crack advancing through the architecture: {architecture}

hint.monolithic: Cast the mineral as one block and a crack runs dead straight along the plane of highest tension. Every millimetre it travels is free.
hint.platelets: Break the block into platelets and the crack has to detour around each one, arriving at every interface with less force than it started with.
hint.bridged: Now let some mineral bridges survive behind the tip. They pull the crack faces shut from behind, and this is roughly where real nacre sits.
hint.bouligand: Rotate each layer a little further than the last. The crack can no longer find a single plane to follow, so it has to corkscrew — the mantis shrimp's club.

verdict.monolithic: This is the baseline, and it is a bad one. Aragonite in bulk is chalky and brittle: a flaw anywhere becomes a crack, and the crack runs to the far side without ever being made to work for it.
verdict.platelets: Geometry alone already buys a great deal. Forcing the crack off the straight plane costs it force at every turn, and the path it has to cut gets longer.
verdict.bridged: Real nacre lands about here: roughly a thousand times the energy to break, out of the same brittle mineral it started with. Not a better ingredient — a better arrangement.
verdict.bouligand: Twisting the stack takes the crack out of the drawing plane entirely. It manufactures new surface faster than it advances, which is the most expensive way to travel a crack can be given.

columnHeightCeiling.title: How tall a trunk can stand on its own weight
columnHeightCeiling.subtitle: Greenhill's buckling height — set the base, the wood, and the gravity
columnHeightCeiling.aria: Column buckling height scale, currently {height} metres
columnHeightCeiling.hint: Notice which slider actually moves the ceiling. Diameter is under a two-thirds power and gravity under a cube root, so widening the base beats changing worlds.

verdict.clears: Ordinary wood clears Hometree's 300 m with room to spare, and it does so on Earth-strength gravity too. Whatever stops a real tree at 130 m, it is not buckling — it is getting water to the top.
verdict.fails: At this base diameter the column buckles under its own weight before it reaches 300 m. Widen the base: it is the cheapest fix by far, which is why real giants flare at the bottom.

sparMassFractionGate.title: What a 25-metre wing costs its owner
sparMassFractionGate.subtitle: Swap the spar material and watch the wing eat the animal
sparMassFractionGate.aria: Wing spar mass at {pct} percent of body mass
sparMassFractionGate.hint: The wing has to survive the bending moment and still leave room for a body. Both conditions have to hold at once.

readout.safetyThin: thin — one hard turn from breaking

verdict.viable: This flier works. The spars are light enough to leave a body around them and strong enough to bank hard without breaking.
verdict.grounded: This flier cannot exist. Either the spar breaks under the manoeuvre, or it weighs so much that there is no mass budget left for muscle, gut and brain.
verdict.compare: With {material} instead, the spars would come to {pct}% of body mass.
